nodes.label: Discipline history & scope
nodes.one_line: Trace ethnomusicology from 1880s comparative musicology (Stumpf, Hornbostel) and Bartók and Kodály's folk-music collecting, through Merriam's The Anthropology of Music (1964) and Nettl's surveys, and place any current research question in that lineage.
know_what: comparative musicology — the 1880s Berlin tradition of Stumpf and Hornbostel, which treated non-Western music as a measurable object and collected it on wax cylinders for the Phonogramm-Archiv
folk-music collecting — Bartók and Kodály's turn-of-the-century Hungarian fieldwork, transcribing peasant song from phonograph recordings and insisting the collector know the repertory firsthand
The Anthropology of Music (1964) — Merriam's turn from sound to culture: music studied as human behavior, with the tripartite model of conceptualization, behavior, and sound
bi-musicality — Mantle Hood's 1960s UCLA program requiring students to learn to perform the tradition they study, not merely describe it
cantometrics — Lomax's coding system rating song performance on 37 scales to compare singing styles worldwide (Folk Song Style and Culture, 1968)
the emic/etic distinction — Pike's terms borrowed from linguistics (insider categories vs analyst categories), the frame of the field's longest-running debate
How Musical Is Man (1973) — Blacking's argument that music is 'humanly organized sound,' broadening the object of study beyond art music
Nettl's surveys — The Study of Ethnomusicology (1983, 2005) and the earlier surveys that stabilized the discipline's self-definition and history
the Society for Ethnomusicology (SEM) — founded 1955, publisher of Ethnomusicology, the field's professional home and its standard-bearer
RILM Abstracts of Music Literature — the annotated bibliography of music scholarship since 1967, the entry point for finding who has already worked a tradition
know_how: Place any current research question in the lineage: name which school's questions it answers and which canonical works it builds on or breaks with
Date the major turns — 1880s comparative musicology, SEM 1955, Merriam 1964, Hood's bi-musicality program 1960s, Lomax's cantometrics 1960s-70s — and attach a work to each date
Trace a practice (recording, transcription, collaboration) from its wax-cylinder origin to its current digital form in two or three sentences
Distinguish the schools by what each preserves and what it gives up, using the four-school map: scientific, interpretive, applied, documentary
Find the canonical statement of any sub-debate — emic/etic, prescriptive/descriptive, music in culture vs music as culture — and cite who wrote it and when
Read an old recording study or transcription and identify which school's assumptions produced it, naming the tell
habits: When a claim about a tradition appears, ask which school's frame produced it before accepting it
Date every major work you cite, because a 1964 claim and an 1880s claim do different work
Before fieldwork, rehearse your own project's lineage: what it borrows and what it rejects
Locate each new ethnography in the history before judging its method
Treat 'the field has always done X' as a claim to check against the history, not a reason
nodes.checkpoint: Given a current ethnomusicology article, write a paragraph placing it in the lineage — which school's questions it answers, which canonical works it cites (Merriam, Nettl, Hood, Lomax, Blacking, or their heirs), and what it adds or rejects — that a colleague can verify against the sources.
nodes.common_failure: Learning the history as a parade of names and dates — Stumpf, Merriam, 1964 — without the arguments, so you can recite the canon but cannot say why the field abandoned comparative musicology's assumptions, or which school's frame your own project sits in.
sources: Merriam, The Anthropology of Music (1964)
Nettl, The Study of Ethnomusicology (2005)
Mantle Hood, 'The Challenge of Bi-Musicality' (1960)
Lomax, Folk Song Style and Culture (1968)
Blacking, How Musical Is Man (1973)

nodes.label: Fieldwork preparation
nodes.one_line: Produce a fieldwork plan — site, duration, contacts, recording kit, budget, and IRB timeline — that a supervisor could execute, before you leave home.
know_what: the fieldwork plan — site, duration, contacts, recording kit, budget, and IRB timeline, written as a document someone else could execute
the IRB timeline — 4-12 weeks of institutional review at most universities, so the protocol is drafted and submitted before departure, not after arrival
gatekeepers — the elders, ritual leaders, and festival organizers whose permission unlocks access to a music community
the recording kit — a portable recorder (e.g., Zoom H5), spares, windscreen, headphones, and backup storage, runnable from memory
budget categories — travel, accommodation, per diem, interpreter days, and the convention of paying consultants for their time and knowledge
the study's one-sentence purpose — the research questions every plan decision (site, duration, kit) must serve
know_how: Write the plan as a document a supervisor could execute: site, dates, named contacts, kit, budget table, IRB timeline, and a day-by-day field schedule
Draft the IRB protocol and consent forms in the consultants' language before departure, leaving room for the board's revisions
Research the site's music calendar — festival cycles, ritual seasons, practice schedules — and schedule arrival around real performance dates, not convenience
Run a full field-day rehearsal at home: pack, record, transfer, back up, so no component is tested for the first time abroad
Cost the study honestly — per diem, transport, spares, interpreter days, consultant honoraria — with a 15-20% contingency
Budget the exit plan — how recordings and findings return to the community — so reciprocity is planned, not improvised
habits: Test every piece of gear before it goes in the bag, and pack spares for anything that fails silently
Keep the IRB clock on the calendar in weeks, not months — 4-12 weeks of review is real lead time
Write down every open question a plan element raises (a contact, a date) and chase it before departure
Rehearse the consent conversation in the consultants' language until it is natural, not recited
Re-read the study's purpose before every plan revision and cut anything that does not serve it
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a one-page fieldwork plan — site, dates, named contacts, kit list with spares, budget with a 15-20% contingency, and an IRB timeline with submission and approval dates — that a supervisor signs off as executable.
nodes.common_failure: Planning the trip but not the ethics: booking travel and packing the recorder while the 4-12 week IRB clock is still running, so fieldwork starts without approved protocols and every recording is unusable as evidence.
sources: Barz & Cooley, Shadows in the Field (2nd ed., 2008)
SEM position statement on fieldwork ethics
45 CFR 46 (Common Rule) and your institution's IRB guidance

nodes.label: Field recording
nodes.one_line: Field-record a live performance with a portable recorder (e.g., Zoom H5) at usable levels and clean sound — no clipping, no wind rumble, no dead batteries — in one take.
know_what: the Zoom H5 or equivalent portable recorder — the field standard, with two XLR inputs, interchangeable capsules, and SD-card capture
record level — input gain set so peaks sit around -12 to -6 dBFS: hot enough to use, with headroom against a sudden fortissimo
clipping — the distortion when a peak crosses 0 dBFS, unrecoverable in post; the one failure no EQ can fix
wind rumble — subsonic pressure noise cut by a foam or furry windscreen before the diaphragm, not fixable afterward
96 kHz/24-bit WAV — the capture format that preserves dynamic headroom and detail for archival use; 44.1 kHz/16-bit is a downgrade you cannot undo
BWF — Broadcast Wave Format, the WAV wrapper carrying a timestamp and metadata chunk that archives use to identify a take
stereo technique — for most field recording, a fixed XY or AB pair that captures the room along with the music, not spot mics
backup discipline — transfer cards daily and keep two copies, because a single card is one failure from losing the fieldwork
know_how: Set gain at a soundcheck with the musicians playing at performance level so peaks sit around -12 to -6 dBFS, then leave the gain alone
Run fresh batteries, a charged spare, and a tested card before each session, checking remaining time between takes
Fit the windscreen before any outdoor take and place the recorder 1-3 meters from the sound source, aimed at the ensemble, not the audience
Record a spoken slate — date, place, performers, piece — before each take so the file identifies itself if metadata is lost
Monitor through headphones during the take and re-record immediately on hearing clipping or rumble, rather than hoping to fix it later
Transfer each day's files to two storage devices and verify by checksum before erasing the card
habits: Treat the soundcheck as part of the performance: never start a take without confirming the meters sit in the safe band
Carry spare batteries and cards in the pocket, not the bag, so a mid-ritual swap takes seconds
When in doubt about level, err to the quiet side — -12 dBFS is recoverable in post, clipping is not
Speak the slate even when you think you will remember — you will not, six weeks later
Back up before celebrating: the day is not done until the files exist in two places
nodes.checkpoint: Field-record a live performance in one take with a portable recorder (e.g., Zoom H5): peaks between -12 and -6 dBFS, no clipping or wind rumble, a spoken slate on the file, and the take transferred to two storage devices with a checksum verified.
nodes.common_failure: Trying to fix at the desk what should be fixed at capture: leaving the meter pinned into clipping or the recorder in the wrong position, then discovering the distortion is permanent — no EQ, denoiser, or resampler restores a clipped peak.
sources: Zoom H5 user manual
Bernard Lortat-Jacob, 'Recording' in Ethnomusicology: An Introduction (Myers ed., 1992)
IASA TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects

nodes.label: Transcription & notation fundamentals
nodes.one_line: Transcribe a 30-second recorded passage into readable notation with correct pitches, rhythm, and meter, choosing Western staff notation, LAB shorthand, or a graphical system as the music demands.
know_what: Western staff notation — the five-line default the field still publishes in, built for European art music and prone to distorting other traditions
LAB shorthand — Seeger's letter-name system (A-G, accidentals, barlines) for capturing a melodic line faster than full staff notation
the prescriptive/descriptive distinction — Seeger (1958): prescriptive notation tells a performer what to do, descriptive records what was heard, and no single notation does both
aksak meters — additive, non-isochronous rhythms such as Bulgarian 7/8 (2+2+3) that resist Western barlines and must not be forced into 4/4
sléndro/pélog — Javanese tuning systems off the equal-tempered grid, so pitch accuracy is reported in cents rather than assumed staff positions
the cent — the logarithmic pitch unit (100 cents = one equal-tempered semitone) used to report deviations the staff cannot show
the 30-second passage — the standard transcription unit, worked in 3-5 second loops because the ear cannot hold a longer stretch accurately
ornamentation and microtiming — the inflections Western notation approximates at best, often the features that carry a tradition's identity
know_how: Choose the system from the music, not from habit: staff for pitch-driven art music, LAB for a quick melodic line, graphical (Sonic Visualiser or Praat spectrogram) when the passage defeats both
Transcribe in passes — meter and phrase skeleton first, then pitches, then ornamentation — never note-by-note from the first listen
Loop 3-5 seconds of audio at a time and write what you hear before moving on, checking each completed bar against the recording
Set the meter from the accents you hear — tap along and find where the strong beats fall — before drawing any barlines, keeping aksak groupings intact
Measure uncertain pitches with a tuner and write the deviation in cents rather than rounding to the nearest staff degree
Write a caption naming the notation system, the conventions used, and what is deliberately omitted, so the reader knows what the score claims
Re-listen at half speed when two hearings conflict, and decide which reading the audio actually supports
habits: Ask what the notation is for before choosing it — a score for analysis is not a score for performance
Loop small chunks instead of replaying the whole passage, keeping attention on one decision at a time
Write the meter from the accents you hear, never from the barline you expect
When a pitch sits between staff degrees, write the cents deviation instead of rounding
Keep a commentary column or layer for everything the notation cannot carry, so no information is silently dropped
Re-listen to your own transcription a day later and mark every spot you would now write differently

know_why.claim: Transcription can be a neutral inscription of the recording — a transparent 'text' of the performance that other analysts can read and compare without the transcriber's interpretation getting in the way.
know_why.because: A shared written record is what lets analysts compare traditions and lets readers check claims against the same passage; if every score is a personal reading, comparison loses its common ground.
know_why.disputed_by: the interpretive camp, following Seeger's prescriptive/descriptive distinction and Ellingson's critique, holds that every notation selects, shapes, and analyzes — transcription is interpretation, so the honest move is to make the analysis visible and argue for it, not hide behind a claim of neutrality.
know_why.source: Charles Seeger, 'Prescriptive and Descriptive Music-Writing' (1958); Ter Ellingson, 'Transcription' in Ethnomusicology: An Introduction, ed. Helen Myers (1992)

nodes.checkpoint: Transcribe a 30-second passage you have never heard before into readable notation — pitches, rhythm, and meter verified against the recording, system chosen with a caption stating conventions and omissions — and defend each bar on re-listening.
nodes.common_failure: Reaching for staff notation by default and forcing the music onto its grid: aksak meters squeezed into 4/4, sléndro pitches rounded to tempered semitones, ornamentation dropped as error — a score that looks clean and misrepresents the music.
sources: Charles Seeger, 'Prescriptive and Descriptive Music-Writing' (1958)
Ter Ellingson, 'Transcription' in Ethnomusicology: An Introduction (Myers ed., 1992)
Bartók, Serbo-Croatian Folk Songs (1951)

nodes.label: Formal musical analysis
nodes.one_line: Analyze a transcribed piece for form, scale, rhythm, and timbre, and write up the analysis with labeled examples drawn from your own transcription.
know_what: form — the piece's large-scale layout: strophic, through-composed, A B A, call-and-response, marked by section boundaries a listener can hear
the labeled example — the convention that every analytical claim cites a specific bar or phrase from your own transcription, numbered and quotable
scale — the pitch collection identified from measured intervals and matched against the tradition's own names before importing analyst categories
rhythmic structure — the metrical framework and the repeating timeline (e.g., a West African bell pattern) that the parts relate to
timbre — the sound qualities notation drops (a kora's attack, a throat-singer's overtones) that analysis must recover by listening
motivic repetition — the short cells a piece builds on; locating them is the first move in most formal analysis
call-and-response — the antiphonal structure common across African and African-diaspora music, with its own formal conventions
description vs interpretation — the two registers analysis must keep distinct and label separately in the write-up
know_how: Mark the form first: listen for section boundaries, label them (A, B, refrain), and check the labels against the transcription's phrase structure
Extract the pitch collection from the transcription and compare it with the tradition's own scale names before applying imported categories
Analyze the rhythm from the timeline outward — find the repeating pattern, then how each part relates to it — before describing any part alone
Attach every claim to a labeled example with a bar or timestamp reference a reader can check against the recording
Keep description and interpretation in separate labeled columns in the draft, weaving them only when both are solid
Compare sections or phrases formally — same or different material, how transformed — before claiming anything larger about the piece
Write the analysis with the transcription as an appendix, examples timestamped into the recording
habits: Name the form before anything else — the piece's layout frames every other observation
When a scale or meter looks familiar, check it against the tradition's own categories before importing yours
Quote the music: every analysis paragraph earns a labeled example, or it is not analysis
Label every claim description or interpretation in the notes, keeping the two columns separate
Re-listen to the passage behind each labeled example before finalizing, so the example says what the audio does
nodes.checkpoint: Analyze a transcribed piece for form, scale, rhythm, and timbre and write up the analysis with at least four labeled examples from your own transcription, each with a bar or timestamp reference a reader can verify against the recording.
nodes.common_failure: Analyzing the score instead of the music: reading form and scale off the transcription alone and asserting interpretations with no labeled examples — claims the reader cannot check, because no passage is ever cited.
sources: Jan LaRue, Guidelines for Style Analysis (2nd ed., 1992)
Bruno Nettl, The Study of Ethnomusicology (2005), analytical chapters
Steven Feld, 'Sound Structure as Social Structure' (1984)

nodes.label: Thick description
nodes.one_line: Write a thick-description passage (Geertz) of a performance you observed — action, sound, context, meaning — from your field notes, dense enough to ground a claim.
know_what: thick description — Geertz's term (The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973): action, context, and meaning layered so the reader knows whether it was a wink or a twitch
thin vs thick — a thin account reports what happened; a thick account reports what the happening meant to those doing it
the performance passage — the unit of writing here: one event (a ritual, a rehearsal, a festival set) rendered densely from field notes
the evidential standard — every interpretive sentence traceable to a field-note observation, a recording, or a quote
emic meaning — the participants' own sense of what the music does, which thick description exists to carry
the native's point of view — Malinowski's injunction, the ancestor of Geertz's project and the standing justification for ethnography over surveys
field notes as raw material — no observation recorded, no thickness possible
the single-case warrant — one well-understood performance grounds claims a survey cannot
know_how: Write the passage with the event pinned: time, place, who was there, what you could see and hear
Layer the account — observable action and sound, then the context that makes it legible, then the meanings participants gave it — each layer labeled
Quote consultants by name or role, translated and contextualized, as evidence for every meaning claim
Show, don't summarize: render the kora's attack, the dancer's timing, the elder's remark as particulars a reader can picture
Ground each interpretive sentence in an observation you recorded, and cut any sentence that has no field-note source
Mark what you saw, what you were told, and what you infer, explicitly, within the passage
Write 500-800 words on one event and check that a reader who was not there can reconstruct what happened and what it meant
habits: Turn to the expanded field notes before writing each passage, never writing from memory of the event
Keep the observation layer and the interpretation layer separate in the first draft, weaving them only when both are solid
When a meaning claim has no evidence, flag it as a question for the next visit rather than deleting it silently
Re-read Geertz's Balinese cockfight essay before writing, as the model of the genre
Check every passage against one question: could a participant recognize themselves in this?

know_why.claim: The core product of ethnomusicology is thick description — a dense, interpretive account of music in culture that lets a reader who was not there understand what a performance meant.
know_why.because: Meaning is carried in particulars — a gesture, a tuning, a remark — and only a passage dense enough to carry those particulars can ground a claim about a tradition; analysis without it floats.
know_why.disputed_by: the scientific school, which demands replicable, thin, data-attached accounts — measurable transcripts, coded features, statistics in the style of Lomax's cantometrics — and treats interpretive prose as unverifiable wherever its claims cannot be checked line by line against the data.
know_why.source: Clifford Geertz, 'Thick Description: Toward an Interpretive Theory of Culture' (1973); Alan Lomax, Folk Song Style and Culture (1968); the scientific/interpretive debate running through Ethnomusicology since the 1960s

nodes.checkpoint: Write a 500-800-word thick-description passage of a performance you observed — action, sound, context, and meaning layered from your field notes, every interpretive sentence traceable to a recorded observation — that a reader who was not there can reconstruct.
nodes.common_failure: Writing 'thick' as ornate: stacking vivid adjectives onto a thin factual base, so the passage is atmospheric but its interpretive claims float with no field-note evidence — the exact failure the scientific school cites against the genre.
sources: Clifford Geertz, 'Thick Description: Toward an Interpretive Theory of Culture' (1973)
Steven Feld, Sound and Sentiment (1982)
Bronislaw Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922)

nodes.label: Archive deposit
nodes.one_line: Assemble a complete deposit package — master recordings, metadata, consent and rights records, and the written documentation of the study — and submit it to an archive such as the Archive of World Music, accepted without follow-up questions.
know_what: the deposit package — master recordings, metadata, consent and rights records, and the study's written documentation, handed over as one unit
the Archive of World Music (Harvard) — a major ethnomusicology archive whose deposit guidelines model what a complete package must contain
BWF masters at 96 kHz/24-bit — the preservation format archives accept as masters, per the field's file-standard conventions
access vs preservation copies — the master stays in the archive; users get a lower-resolution access copy
the rights record — signed consent and release forms stating who may hear, quote, and copy each recording
the metadata record — who, what, when, where, instrument, genre, rights, in a standard like Dublin Core; without it a recording is noise
the accession agreement — the contract between depositor and archive defining access restrictions, closure periods, and community rights
the collection record — the finding aid or catalog entry that lets a stranger locate a specific recording
know_how: Assemble the package against the archive's own deposit guidelines, item by item, checking each against its checklist before submission
Prepare the masters in the archive's convention — BWF at 96 kHz/24-bit, checksums computed, files named with accession-ready identifiers
Pair every recording with its metadata record and rights record, so no file enters the archive unaccompanied
State access restrictions explicitly — open, restricted, community-only, closed — in the agreement, honoring what consultants consented to
Write the deposit documentation — study summary, collection overview, recording log — in the archive's expected format
Submit the package, confirm acceptance in writing, and keep the agreement and accession number on file
Arrange the community copy as part of deposit, so return to the community happens at the same moment as preservation
habits: Treat the deposit as the last act of fieldwork, not an admin chore after it
Check the archive's deposit guidelines before assembling, never after
Keep the rights record with the recordings from day one, so consent is never reconstructed from memory
Name files so a stranger can sort them before opening them
Confirm acceptance in writing and file the agreement where the next researcher can find it
Ask the archive how the community can access copies, and build that into the agreement
nodes.checkpoint: Submit a complete deposit package to a real archive (e.g., the Archive of World Music) — BWF masters at 96 kHz/24-bit, metadata and rights records for every item, and written documentation — and receive acceptance without follow-up questions.
nodes.common_failure: Depositing the recordings and nothing else: files arrive with no metadata, no rights records, and no documentation, so the archive returns them with questions — or shelves them as inaccessible noise no future researcher can cite.
sources: Archive of World Music (Harvard) deposit guidelines
IASA TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects
SEM statement on ethics and archival deposit
